extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars studying Milton's Areopagitica (annotated edition)
extracted.subtask_description: Guided, line‑by‑line notes and study prompts for reading, explaining, and analysing Milton's Areopagitica (vocabulary, grammar, historical allusions, and the speech's argumentative structure). Intended to direct close reading and classroom tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify grammatical subject of 'might disclose'
rubrics_metrics.description: '[might disclose. What is the grammatical subject to might disclose ?]'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate the clause containing 'might disclose' and specify which noun or clause functions as its grammatical subject; explain the syntactic relation. (This is an explicit study question in the notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain 'incidentall to a Preface'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the meaning of the phrase 'incidentall to a Preface' in context, and show how it applies to Milton's usage — i.e., what is incidental vs essential to a preface. Provide examples or comparisons to other prefaces if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the construction 'Neither is it, &c.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the grammatical and stylistic function of the construction beginning 'Neither is it...' in the passage (including any punctuation or editorial marks shown as '//'), and clarify how the phrase operates rhetorically in Milton's sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a list of 'your victories and successes' referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: '[19. in the midd'st of your victories and successes. Make a list of these.]'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and enumerate the specific 'victories and successes' alluded to in the speech/context (historical events, political achievements, or rhetorical victories), citing passage locations and brief explanations for each item.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the respective meanings of 'worst' and 'worse'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the worst. It is possible worst may be a misprint for worse; ... [State distinctly the respective meanings.]'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the distinct senses conveyed by 'worst' vs 'worse' in the passage; explain which sense fits Milton's line and why (textual evidence and semantic argument). Note editorial considerations about possible misprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the two different meanings of 'license' and identify the play on words
rubrics_metrics.description: '[22. licence. State clearly the two different meanings oi license, on which there is a play here,]'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the two senses of 'license' in Milton's usage (e.g., licence = permission/regulation vs licence = licentious freedom/unregulated behaviour). Explain how Milton exploits the double meaning rhetorically and give line references illustrating each sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and map the divisions of the Speech (I–IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Observe the divisions of the Speech here proposed. He will point out who are I. The Authors of the book-licensing system, pp. 5-13. II. 'What is to be thought in general of reading books, whatever sort they be, and whether be more the benefit or harm that thence proceeds,' pp. 13-22. III. 'That this order of licensing conduces nothing to the end for which it was framed,' pp. 22-29. IV. It will not only do no good; it will do immense harm in discouraging the pursuit of learning and the search after truth, pp. 29 to end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate the speech by marking these four major sections; for each section summarize the central claim(s), primary evidence or examples Milton uses, and their location in the text. Use the provided page ranges as anchors for mapping argument structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the two forms of the past participle (historical inflection)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[27. catcht . . . caught. Observe the two forms of the past participle.]"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note and explain Milton's (or contemporaneous) use of variant past participle forms (e.g., 'catcht' vs 'caught'). Discuss morphological or dialectal reasoning and any implications for reading/editing the text (is one a compound, is inflection irregular?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask what 'almost' modifies in the clause
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine which word or phrase 'almost' is qualifying in the given sentence; explain how that qualification affects the meaning of the clause and the rhetorical force of the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace and explain historical/pronominal usage distinctions ('ye' vs 'you')
rubrics_metrics.description: 'P. 3, I. 3. ye. 'The confusion between ye and you did not exist in Old English. Ye was always used as a nom., and you as a dat. or ace. ... but in the dramatists ... there is a very loose use of the two forms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the historical grammatical distinction between 'ye' (nominative) and 'you' (objective) and note how later loosening in Early Modern drama affects Milton's usage; give examples from the text and relevant comparative citations (Bible, dramatists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gloss and explain key vocabulary, etymologies, and classical allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the notes the editor glosses words (e.g., 'wanting' = being without; 'alter' = to make other; 'success' = issue; definitions of 'courtship', 'civil', 'polite', 'quintessence', etc.) and gives classical/historical parallels and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each gloss: provide definition, etymology, and any cited parallels (classical authors, Biblical citations, other English authors). Explain how knowledge of these meanings and allusions affects interpretation of Milton's passages; follow the editor's cross-references (Introduction, other Milton works, classical texts).
